title: Streaming chunking, flush & cancellation guidelines
content:
Purpose
This doc captures recommended behaviors and low-level invariants for streaming generation in the serving runtime: chunking rules, flush policies, cancellation semantics, and interactions with the KV cache and scheduler. It's intended to be implementation-guidance for runtime engineers and a reference for product tradeoffs when we tune latency vs quality vs cost.

Context and goals
- Users expect low time-to-first-token and predictable partial-output behaviour for long-running generations (chat, codegen).
- We must avoid emitting malformed partial tokens that downstream parsers or tool-callers can't recover from.
- The runtime must preserve KV-cache correctness when partial outputs are emitted, retried, or cancelled.
- Provide surgeon-level knobs for prioritization (e.g., latency SLOs) while keeping safe defaults.

Design constraints
- Models expose logits at subtoken or token granularity depending on tokenizer/kernels. Some kernels produce BPE-subtoken outputs, others emit whole-token IDs.
- GPU kernels flush output from device to host in batches; too-frequent tiny flushes harm throughput.
- Cancellation requests can arrive from client or internal routing fallback; cancellation should be fast but not cause KV cache corruption.
- Backpressure: clients can read slowly. The runtime must avoid unbounded memory retention of in-flight KV caches or prefix buffers per session.

Key invariants (must hold across implementations)
1) A partial emission must never claim a model token has been committed to KV cache unless the same token will be present in any subsequent resumed execution for that session.
2) Cancellation may drop uncommitted tokens; committed tokens (those integrated into the KV cache state on device) are durable for the session unless a replay/rollback is explicitly performed.
3) Emitted bytes must be decodable by a UTF-8-safe streaming consumer; partial multibyte characters must be buffered until complete.

Chunking strategy (how we split generation for emission)
- Default approach: token-aligned chunking with a soft-subtoken fallback. Prefer emitting at token boundaries.
  - When kernel emits whole-token IDs: flush when a token is marked complete.
  - When kernel emits subtokens: buffer subtokens until either (a) token-complete marker, or (b) soft-timeout reached and the policy allows partial-subtoken emission for low-latency mode.
- Chunk size target: 32-128 tokens per flush under throughput mode; for latency-mode we target smaller chunks (1-8 tokens), but subject to flush cost heuristics.
- For very long tokens (e.g., 100+ subtokens), treat as a spanning token: prefer incremental subtoken flush but annotate emissions with a stable token boundary flag when first seen.

Flush policy (when to send buffered output to client)
We define a layered policy with three triggers: completion trigger, time trigger, and scheduler trigger.
- Completion trigger: token boundary or EOS; strongest signal. Always flush.
- Time trigger: if buffered output hasn't been flushed after T_ms. Two T_ms profiles:
  - default (balanced): T_ms = 50 ms
  - low-latency: T_ms = 10-20 ms (aggressive; may increase GPU overhead)
- Scheduler trigger: when scheduler decides to preempt, migrate, or reallocate resources, it may request an immediate flush of the active buffer so the receiving process has the latest prefix. This is required before migrating a session off device.
Implementation notes:
- Prefer coalescing flushes when multiple sessions on same device are ready within 1-2ms window to amortize PCIe/device-host transfer costs.
- Always attach metadata with flush: sequence_id, last_committed_token_index, flush_type (token_boundary|partial_subtoken|forced_preempt), and kernel_generation_id. These are opaque strings in the stream but required for debugging and safe resume.

Partial-subtoken emission rules
- Only allowed if client explicitly enables subtoken-streaming in request (opt-in). Default is token-only streaming.
- When enabled, subtokens are emitted only after ensuring the byte-level encoding is UTF-8-safe. If a subtoken ends with an incomplete UTF-8 byte sequence, buffer until the rest arrives.
- Every partial emission must include a stable prefix hash (32-bit) that the client can use to detect truncated or reordered chunks.

Cancellation semantics
We define two cancellation levels the runtime must support: graceful (soft) and immediate (hard).
- Soft cancellation (default): client requests cancellation but allows the generator to finish the current token (or the current subtoken window if enabled) and flush the result. Use-case: preserve syntactic integrity for downstream parsers. Latency: small additional time.
- Hard cancellation: stop execution at earliest safe point; do not flush uncommitted partial subtokens. Required for strict SLO preemption.

KV cache interactions and correctness
- Commit rule: token is considered "committed" to KV cache when the kernel has integrated token's key/value pairs into the device-side KV store and the runtime records a committed_token_index for the session. Committed tokens survive cancellation unless a rollback is triggered by a deterministic replay.
- Flushing must not auto-commit tokens unless kernel commit completes. Emission metadata must include last_committed_token_index so the client can differentiate between emitted-only vs committed tokens.
- On cancellation, behavior: 
  - Soft cancel: finish and commit current token (if commit completes) and flush.
  - Hard cancel: do not commit the in-progress token; mark it as dropped and ensure any partially allocated device KV slots are reclaimed in the next GC cycle to avoid leaks.
- Resume semantics: if a session resumes after cancellation and some tokens were only emitted (not committed), runtime should optionally support replay: reapply the emitted token IDs to rederive KV state and continue. Replay is expensive — flag as opt-in (resume_with_replay=true).

Scheduler interactions and prioritization
- Scheduler must be aware of streaming state flags: is_streaming, soft_cancel_allowed, low_latency_profile. These influence scheduling decisions: e.g., prefer colocating low-latency sessions to reduce transfer overhead.
- Preemptions: before migrating a session, scheduler issues "preempt_flush" to kernel; kernel responds with flush metadata (last_committed_token, outstanding_buffer_bytes). Migration waits for flush ACK or times out after scheduler-configured deadline.
- Fairness: too-aggressive flushing from many low-latency sessions can starve batch throughput. Scheduler must enforce a token-budget per-device for tiny flushes and fall back to batched flush window when budget exhausted.

Edge cases and failure modes
- Device crash mid-flush: use persistent host-side session journal with last_committed_token_index to recover and rehydrate KV cache on next allocation.
- Slow client reads: if client read window is full, we must apply backpressure and optionally throttle model generation. TTL-based session eviction for idle read-blocked sessions (configurable) to avoid resource hogging.
- Partial UTF-8 / emoji sequences across subtokens: buffer until full codepoint; do not emit incomplete codepoints.

Metrics and observability
Track these per-session and per-model metrics:
- time_to_first_flush_ms
- flush_interval_distribution_ms
- bytes_per_flush
- committed_tokens_vs_emitted_tokens_ratio
- cancellations_soft_vs_hard counts and cause tags
- resume_with_replay_frequency
- flush_retries_due_to_preemptions
Include flush metadata in traces for correlating with scheduler decisions and kernel logs.

Experiments and rollout plan
- Phase A (lab): implement token-aligned chunking + default 50ms time trigger. Run against existing chat and codegen benchmarks; measure throughput and TTF (time-to-first).
- Phase B (canary): expose low-latency toggle to 5% of traffic; enable subtoken-streaming opt-in for telemetry clients. Evaluate device CPU/GPU overhead and increase in PCIe transactions.
- Phase C (gradual): add scheduler token-budget and preempt_flush coordination, enable by default in regions with high latency sensitivity.

Open questions and tradeoffs
- Should replay-on-resume be enabled by default for Hosted API? (cost vs user-visible integrity)
- How aggressive should preempt_flush timeouts be when migrating; tradeoff between migration speed and consistency guarantees.
- Whether to expose partial-subtoken streaming to public API or keep as internal opt-in only.

Implementation checklist (developer-facing)
- [ ] Add per-session flush buffer with metadata (sequence_id, last_committed_token_index).
- [ ] Implement coalesced device->host flush queue with 1-2ms batching window.
- [ ] Add soft/hard cancellation API hooks in session manager and scheduler.
- [ ] Add host-side session journal for last_committed_token_index durability.
- [ ] Emit flush metadata into tracing span and logs.

Notes to reviewers
- This doc intentionally prefers token-boundary safety as the default; subtoken emission is opt-in because it complicates correctness and increases device-host transfer overhead.
- Feedback needed on default time trigger values and whether the scheduler token-budget should be global or per-device.
- See linked artifacts for prior experiments and a related PR that added kernel-level partial-subtoken markers.

Appendix: example wire-level flush envelope (informal)
{
  sequence_id: "s-12345",
  flush_type: "token_boundary",
  last_committed_token_index: "42",
  token_ids: [101, 345, ...],
  metadata: { model: "rw-l1.2b", kernel_generation_id: "kgen-99" }
}
(Implementation should serialize this into the streaming envelope; ensure field names are stable across releases.)

End of doc
